disease_info: Binge-Eating Disorder is characterized by recurrent episodes of eating large quantities of food in a discrete period while experiencing a sense of loss of control, typically accompanied by marked distress and guilt afterward. Unlike bulimia nervosa, it is not regularly followed by inappropriate compensatory behaviors such as vomiting, fasting, or excessive exercise, and it is often associated with overweight or obesity but can occur at any weight. The course can be chronic or fluctuating, frequently emerging in the context of dieting, weight stigma, emotional stress, or long-standing patterns of using food to regulate affect. It commonly co-occurs with mood and anxiety disorders and can significantly impair psychosocial functioning and quality of life even when not perceived as severe by the individual.

narrative.personality: Elizabeth is a routine-driven, sociable, and competitive craftsperson who values thrift and structure but can be stubborn and indulgent with certain personal comforts.
narrative.stressor: About six months ago, Elizabeth took a financial risk by downsizing her general contracting work to focus on building a boutique custom furniture studio and teaching more classes, which disrupted the predictable routines she has relied on for decades. The new venture brought irregular income, long solitary hours in the shop catching up on commissions, and pressure to prove that her late-career pivot was not a mistake, especially as peers her age were talking about retirement. As she stayed later in the studio and skipped regular meals, she fell into a pattern of bringing home large amounts of takeout or potluck leftovers and eating mechanically while exhausted, telling herself it was a way to unwind after pushing her body all day. Over the next four months, this pattern became more frequent, and she finally sought help after noticing she was planning her evenings around these episodes, feeling physically uncomfortable during the night and worried it was starting to sap her energy for work and community theater.
narrative.chief_complaint: I keep eating past the point of feeling full, to where I’m really uncomfortable afterward.

narrative.personality: Yong Ho is a conscientious, detail-oriented medical assistant who enjoys cooking, music, and mindfulness but tends to overthink finances and worry about making mistakes.
narrative.stressor: Four months ago, Yong Ho’s roommate moved out unexpectedly, forcing him to take on a much larger share of the rent just as his clinic cut overtime hours, which intensified his preexisting worries about money and job security. To save on costs, he started cooking in bulk and staying home more, spending long evenings alone after stressful days at the clinic, where he constantly worried about the accuracy of his work. Over time, he fell into a habit of repeatedly returning to the kitchen in the late evenings, eating from the meals he had prepared even when he wasn’t physically hungry, telling himself it was a small comfort he could still afford. He decided to seek psychiatric help when he realized these eating patterns were becoming a near-nightly ritual, leaving him feeling sluggish for morning shifts and conflicted about his health despite his medical knowledge.
narrative.chief_complaint: I find myself eating a lot of food in the evenings even when I’m not actually hungry.

narrative.personality: Alixe is an organized, calm, and analytical supervisor who enjoys structure, gardening, and mindfulness practices, yet has a soft spot for indulging in new tools and small personal luxuries.
narrative.stressor: Roughly five months ago, Alixe injured her knee during a weekend hike, which led to reduced mobility and her doctor advising her to significantly cut back on walking and yoga for several months. Losing her usual outlets for stress relief and physical activity was particularly destabilizing for her, given how much she relies on structured routines and movement to stay centered while managing a demanding housekeeping team. As she spent more time at home resting with her leg elevated and less time in her garden or at community clean-ups, she began cooking and snacking more out of boredom and to recreate a sense of reward after difficult days at work, often eating well beyond any physical need for food. After about four months of this pattern, she became concerned that these behaviors were persisting even as her knee improved and that they were starting to affect her energy and confidence at work, prompting her to seek psychiatric evaluation.
narrative.chief_complaint: I’ve gotten into this pattern of eating a lot even when I know I’m not actually hungry, and it’s starting to worry me.
